report:
## Conclusion

No — hydroxychloroquine does **not** reduce mortality from COVID-19, and current evidence indicates it provides no meaningful clinical benefit for hospitalized or non-hospitalized patients.

Multiple large, high-quality randomized controlled trials have tested this question directly. The UK's **RECOVERY trial**, one of the largest and most rigorous COVID-19 trials (over 1,500 patients randomized to hydroxychloroquine vs. usual care), found no reduction in 28-day mortality, no reduction in hospital stay, and no improvement in the likelihood of avoiding invasive mechanical ventilation or death (NEJM, https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2022926). Based on these findings, RECOVERY halted its hydroxychloroquine arm as futile.

The **WHO Solidarity Trial**, an international multi-country RCT, similarly found that hydroxychloroquine "produced little or no reduction" in mortality among hospitalized COVID-19 patients compared to standard care, leading WHO to discontinue that treatment arm as well (https://www.nejm.org/doi/10.1056/NEJMoa2023184).

A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials pooling this and other trial data concluded that hydroxychloroquine showed no mortality benefit and, in some analyses, was associated with a possible signal of harm rather than benefit (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8013604/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8220439/).

Earlier observational studies suggesting benefit were generally lower-quality, subject to confounding, or in some high-profile cases (e.g., the retracted Lancet study) methodologically flawed. The scientific consensus based on RCT evidence—the gold standard for causal treatment effects—is clear and consistent across independent trials and regulatory bodies (FDA, WHO): hydroxychloroquine does not reduce COVID-19 mortality and is not recommended for treating or preventing COVID-19.
